children: Holtec Nuclear, which is on track to be the first company to bring a defunct nuclear power plant back to life, is looking to raise about $900 million in an initial public offering that could value it at more than $10 billion.

Holtec is a unique firm in the nuclear industry. It's been around for 40 years and is best known for decommissioning old reactors and making casks to store spent nuclear waste. Those operations aren't very sexy, but they generate steady profits. The company reported net income of $387 million last year on $577 million in revenue.

But Holtec has also been getting into new business lines that it expects to be major money-makers in the years ahead. It is on the brink of restarting a nuclear reactor in Michigan known as Palisades, which stopped operating in 2022.

The company had initially purchased the site with the intention of decommissioning it. But federal and state governments didn't want to lose the power that Palisades provided and agreed to chip in funding to get it back online. It's expected to be fully commissioned by the end of the year and provide enough power for up to 800,000 homes next year. Holtec expects Palisades "will give a steady stream of income to us for three decades."

Holtec is also working on another new business venture: building its own small reactors. It's already planning to put two of the smaller reactors at Palisades, subject to regulatory approval, and sees opportunities to add them elsewhere, too. Because of its decommissioning work, Holtec owns several defunct nuclear sites that could eventually host its new reactors.

It's already discussing plans to place small reactors at a site known as Oyster Creek near the Atlantic Ocean in New Jersey. The company's IPO filing also floats the idea of building reactors at other defunct nuclear sites, including Indian Point just north of New York City. A nuclear plant there closed in 2021 after strong pushback from local residents.
Holtec is also working with foreign governments, including those of Ukraine and the United Kingdom, on building plants in those countries.

In the past two years, several nuclear companies have gone public, hoping to cash in on a renewed appetite for the power source from tech companies seeking electricity for their AI data centers. The industry has also benefited from billions of dollars in government support.

Holtec is competing against a growing number of small reactor developers, some of which have inked deals with large tech firms like Amazon to provide energy to their data centers. They include X-Energy and Oklo. Nuclear developer Westinghouse has also filed papers to go public, in what's likely to be the largest nuclear IPO in years.
Barron's broke the news about Holtec's plans to go public last year.

Holtec shareholders may be able to benefit from the growth of the nuclear industry, but they won't have much say in the direction of the company. The company will be controlled by founder and CEO Krishna Singh through his control of a holding firm that owns the company's Class B shares, which have 10 times the voting power of Class A shares available to the public.
Singh is expected to become chairman, and his wife, Martha Singh, will be vice chairman. Under the company's rules, they can't be ousted from their roles by regular shareholders.
The stock will be listed under the ticker HNUC on the Nasdaq Global Select Market and Nasdaq Texas. It is expected to start trading this month.
